302.title: A very narrow bridge
302.hook: Rebbe Nachman: the whole world is a very narrow bridge, and the main thing is not to be afraid
302.howItsDone: The song Kol ha-olam kulo, set to Rebbe Nachman's words, is sung at weddings, camps, memorials and gatherings; Breslov Hasidim study his teachings in Likutei Moharan.

segments.voice: Yesterday: cheshbon, an accounting, and a tailor who turned the ledger both ways on Yom Kippur.

Arms around shoulders at a Jewish wedding, a summer camp, a youth group: a roomful of people swaying to a slow Hebrew song. Kol ha-olam kulo, gesher tzar me'od. The whole world is a very narrow bridge. And the main thing is not to be afraid at all. The tune is easy to learn. The source takes a little more digging: a Hasidic master who died young, who wrote openly about sadness, and whose actual words are a little different from the song.
screen: `ARMS AROUND SHOULDERS, SWAYING.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD IS A NARROW BRIDGE.` → `WHERE DO THE WORDS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Rebbe Nachman of Breslov was, the tradition says, a great-grandson of the Baal Shem Tov, whose stories you've been hearing. He lived in Ukraine and died young, in the town of Uman. His student Nathan wrote down his teachings in a book called Likutei Moharan. In one passage, Rebbe Nachman says, roughly: know that a person has to cross a very, very narrow bridge, and the rule and the main thing is not to frighten yourself at all. Much later, a songwriter turned that into the song, and changed it a little on the way. The song makes the whole world the bridge, and says, don't be afraid. The original is subtler. Some readers point to the form of the Hebrew verb, which can be heard as reflexive: don't make yourself afraid. Fear may come; standing over a drop, it usually does. What you can refuse is to feed it, to stand there frightening yourself with every way you might fall. Notice what the teaching doesn't say. It doesn't say the bridge is wide, or that you won't wobble. The path really is narrow, and you still have to cross it. His teachings speak openly about sadness and heaviness of spirit, and he also taught that it is a great mitzvah to be joyful always. Not because life is easy, but because joy is how you keep walking. So the bridge isn't a promise of safety. It's permission to be scared and move anyway.
screen: `NACHMAN OF BRESLOV, IN UMAN.` · `A VERY, VERY NARROW BRIDGE.` · `DON'T MAKE YOURSELF AFRAID.` · `SCARED, AND WALKING ANYWAY.` · then, large: `NOT AFRAID AT ALL.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been avoiding because it scares you: a phone call, a doctor's appointment, an apology, a conversation. Don't try to stop the fear; just notice when you start frightening yourself with stories about how it'll go, and picture only the first step, one plank, not the whole bridge. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to take it.
Rebbe Nachman, whose picture of life was a very narrow bridge: the way across is narrow, and the main thing is not to make yourself afraid.
Your line: not afraid at all. Fear may come; you don't have to feed it. That's day three hundred two.

303.title: The lost princess
303.hook: Rebbe Nachman's tale of a viceroy who searches for years for a lost princess
303.howItsDone: Rebbe Nachman's thirteen tales, collected as Sippurei Ma'asiyot, are read and studied by Breslov Hasidim and many others, often with commentaries that explain their hidden meanings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rebbe Nachman's very narrow bridge, and the main thing, not to make yourself afraid. Today, the same rebbe tells a story, the first of his famous tales.

One careless sentence, said in anger, and a king loses his daughter. That's how the first of Rebbe Nachman's tales begins. He didn't only teach. In his last years he started telling stories, fairy tales really: kings and princesses, giants, deserts, enchanted palaces. They can sound like bedtime stories. He treated them as anything but: his student Nathan wrote them down, and Breslov tradition reads them as teachings in disguise.
screen: `ONE CARELESS SENTENCE.` → `A REBBE TELLS FAIRY TALES.` → `KINGS, GIANTS, PALACES.`

segments.voice: Here's the story, in short strokes. A king has a daughter he loves dearly. One day, angry with her, he blurts out: may the not-good take you. The next morning, she's gone. The king is heartbroken. His viceroy, his second-in-command, asks for a servant, a horse and some money, and sets out to find her. He searches for years. At last he finds her, held in a strange palace. She tells him how to free her: choose a place, long for her for a whole year, and on the last day, fast and stay awake. On the last day, he sees an apple, eats it, and falls into a deep sleep. He fails. She gives him a second chance: this time he may eat, but he must not drink wine. He finds a spring that looks and smells like wine, drinks, and sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, she's been taken farther away. All that's left is her kerchief, with a message written in her tears: now look for me on a mountain of gold, in a castle of pearl. So he gets up and keeps searching, through deserts and giants. The tale's last line is strange: how he freed her, the story doesn't tell. But in the end, he freed her. Breslov teachers read the princess as the Divine Presence in exile, and the viceroy as every person who has lost something holy and is trying to find it again. He isn't a hero because he never fails. He fails twice, badly. He's a hero because the story always says the same thing next: and he kept searching.
screen: `ONE ANGRY SENTENCE.` · `YEARS OF SEARCHING.` · `AN APPLE. A SPRING. SEVENTY YEARS.` · `A MESSAGE WRITTEN IN TEARS.` · then, large: `KEEP SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: Think of something good you once had and lost track of: a friendship, a habit, a sense of wonder, a way of praying. Don't scold yourself for falling asleep on it; the viceroy slept seventy years and still got up. Just ask where you might look for it now, one place, one small first step, and if you pray, ask for help finding it.
Viceroy, the king's second-in-command who set out to find a lost princess in Rebbe Nachman's first tale, failing, sleeping, waking, and searching until he found what was lost.
Your line: keep searching. Failing twice, even sleeping seventy years, doesn't end the story. See you tomorrow.

304.title: The turkey prince
304.hook: a prince thinks he's a turkey, and a sage sits under the table with him
304.howItsDone: The turkey prince parable is retold in Breslov circles, Jewish schools and sermons, often as a lesson in patience and in meeting people where they are.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the viceroy, who failed twice, slept seventy years, and kept searching.

Remember the last time you tried to help someone who didn't want help. A friend spiraling. A teenager who wouldn't talk. A parent refusing to see the doctor. You stood over them with good advice, and the more right you were, the more they dug in. Rebbe Nachman told a short, funny parable about exactly that: a royal family, a dining table, and a prince who has decided he is a turkey. It's one of the most loved stories in the Breslov tradition, still retold in classrooms and therapy offices.
screen: `HELPING SOMEONE WHO WON'T BE HELPED.` → `THE MORE RIGHT YOU ARE…` → `A PRINCE WHO THINKS HE'S A TURKEY.`

segments.voice: A prince goes mad. He decides he's a turkey. He takes off his clothes, crawls under the table, and pecks at crumbs on the floor. The king calls every doctor in the land. They argue with him, they order him, they try every cure. Nothing. Then a wise man comes and says: let me try. He takes off his own clothes, crawls under the table, and starts pecking crumbs. The prince stares. Who are you? A turkey, says the wise man. And you? Also a turkey. So they sit together, two turkeys, and become friends. After a while, the wise man asks for a shirt. The prince is shocked. Who says a turkey can't wear a shirt? You can wear a shirt and still be a turkey. So they both put on shirts. Later, trousers. Later, real food from the table: you can eat good food and still be a turkey. Then one day: you can sit at the table and still be a turkey. Little by little, the prince lives like a prince again. The Yiddish word for turkey is hindik, and Breslov Hasidim still call this the hindik story. Teachers read it on more than one level. On the plain level, it's about how to help: don't shout from the chair. Get under the table. Start where the other person is, and move one step at a time. On a deeper level, many read it about the soul: nobody jumps from the floor to the table in one leap.
screen: `A PRINCE UNDER THE TABLE.` · `THE WISE MAN: ALSO A TURKEY.` · `A SHIRT, THEN TROUSERS, THEN FOOD.` · `ONE STEP AT A TIME.` · then, large: `SIT UNDER THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you've been trying to change, or fix, or talk sense into, and stop standing over them and get down to where they are. What does the world look like from under their table, what are they afraid of, what would make them feel a little less alone? Don't plan a speech; look for one small thing you could share, the way the wise man shared the floor, and if you pray, pray for them.
Hindik, Yiddish for turkey: Rebbe Nachman's parable of a wise man who got under the table with a prince who thought he was one.
Your line: sit under the table. The prince came back one shirt at a time. Day three hundred four, done.

305.title: Where is God?
305.hook: the Kotzker rebbe: God dwells wherever we let Him in
305.howItsDone: In the Kedushah, said aloud in the synagogue's repetition of the Amidah, the congregation proclaims Isaiah's line that the whole earth is full of God's glory; the Kotzker's saying is often quoted in sermons on sincerity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hindik: a wise man got under the table with a turkey prince, and brought him back one step at a time.

Where is God? Up in the sky? In the synagogue? Everywhere? It's the kind of question a child asks at bedtime, and one quick answer is always ready: everywhere. It's a good answer. It's even in the Bible. But one Hasidic rebbe, famous for being fierce, blunt and impossible to please, heard that answer from a room full of learned men, and told them they had it only half right.
screen: `A BEDTIME QUESTION.` → `THE QUICK ANSWER: EVERYWHERE.` → `ONLY HALF RIGHT?`

segments.voice: Menachem Mendel of Kotzk was a Hasidic rebbe in Poland, known for a hatred of anything fake. He wanted truth, all of it, and he could be harsh about it. The story goes that he once surprised a group of learned guests with a question: where does God live? They laughed. What a thing to ask! Isaiah already answered it. The angels call out: "the whole earth is full of His glory." The rebbe answered his own question. God lives wherever people let Him in. He isn't denying the verse. The whole earth may be full of glory, but a person can walk right through it and notice nothing. You can stand in a beautiful place and be somewhere else entirely: inside your phone, your worry, your pride. The door opens from the inside. In the Kedushah said on Shabbat and festivals, the congregation says Isaiah's line, and a little later the prayer pictures the angels asking each other: where is the place of His glory? Ayeh mekom kevodo. The answer comes from Ezekiel's vision: blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place. The question sits right next to the answer. Jewish tradition holds both at once: God fills the world, and God can feel absent. For the Kotzker, what closes the distance isn't a map or a building. It's a person who stops pretending, and makes room for something larger.
screen: `THE KOTZKER: NOTHING FAKE.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL OF GLORY.` · `WHEREVER PEOPLE LET HIM IN.` · `AYEH: WHERE?` · then, large: `WHEREVER YOU LET HIM IN.`

segments.voice: Notice where you're closed right now: rushing, guarded, carrying a grudge, or pretending everything is fine. Don't force anything open; just loosen one latch, breathe into the tight place, and leave a little room. If you pray, invite God in, in your own words or with Isaiah's line; if you don't, let the room fill with whatever is good and true right here.
Kotzker, nickname for Menachem Mendel of Kotzk. His answer to where is God: wherever people let Him in. The earth is full of glory, and the door opens from the inside.
Your line: wherever you let him in. The glory is already here; the latch is on your side. See you tomorrow.

306.title: The crying baby
306.hook: Shneur Zalman leaves his prayer to rock a crying baby his absorbed son never heard
306.howItsDone: Chabad Hasidim tell this story about their first and second rebbes, and it is retold in Jewish homes and schools as a reminder that study and prayer should not make a person deaf to others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kotzker: God lives wherever people let Him in, and the door opens from the inside.

Someone so deep in their laptop they don't hear their name called three times. A parent on the phone while a toddler tugs and tugs at their sleeve. Maybe that someone was you. Deep focus is a gift. It's how books get written and problems get solved. But it has a shadow. Today's story is about a great scholar, lost in holy study, who missed a sound that mattered more, and about his father, who didn't.
screen: `DEEP IN THE LAPTOP.` → `A TODDLER TUGGING A SLEEVE.` → `FOCUS HAS A SHADOW.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi founded the Chabad movement and wrote the Tanya, the book at its heart. The story is told that he lived in a house with his son, Dov Ber, who would later lead Chabad after him. One night Dov Ber was downstairs, completely absorbed in study. In the same room, his baby fell out of the cradle and began to cry. Dov Ber didn't hear a thing. Upstairs, Shneur Zalman was deep in his own study and prayer. He heard the crying. He stopped, came down the stairs, picked the baby up, soothed the child, and laid it back in the cradle. His son never looked up. Afterward, the father spoke to him. However lofty your learning, he said, if it keeps you from hearing a child cry, something has gone wrong. Look who's saying it: not a critic of study, but the founder of a movement built on deep, intense contemplation. He isn't saying stop learning. He's saying learning that makes you deaf to a crying child has lost its way. The Talmud says something in the same spirit: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence, based on Abraham leaving God's company to run to three strangers. Holiness that can't hear a baby isn't finished yet.
screen: `SHNEUR ZALMAN, FOUNDER OF CHABAD.` · `A SON TOO ABSORBED TO HEAR.` · `A FATHER WHO COMES DOWNSTAIRS.` · `LEARNING THAT HEARS.` · then, large: `THE CRYING CHILD FIRST.`

segments.voice: For a moment, listen not to your thoughts but to the room: the sounds outside, someone nearby, your own body, thirsty, tired or tense. Then think of the people around you today, and who might be tugging at your sleeve, quietly, unnoticed. Pick one, and if you pray, pray for them.
Shneur Zalman, who stopped his own holy study to comfort a crying baby his son never heard. Holiness that hears.
Your line: the crying child first. The work can wait; the crying can't. Day three hundred six.

307.title: To know what hurts
307.hook: Moshe Leib of Sassov learned love from a peasant: how can you love me if you don't know what hurts me?
307.howItsDone: Moshe Leib of Sassov's tavern story is often told in Jewish teaching on the command to love one's neighbor, as a reminder that love means paying attention to another person's pain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shneur Zalman came downstairs for a crying baby his son never heard: the crying child first.

Love you. Love you too. How many times have you said it this month? To a partner, a parent, a kid, a friend at the end of a phone call. It's a good habit. But here's a harder question. Of the people you said it to, do you know what's hurting them right now? Not in general. This week. Today's story is about a rebbe who said he learned what love means, not from a book, but from overhearing two men in a tavern.
screen: `LOVE YOU. LOVE YOU TOO.` → `WHAT'S HURTING THEM THIS WEEK?` → `A LESSON FROM A TAVERN.`

segments.voice: Moshe Leib of Sassov was a Hasidic rebbe in Galicia, remembered for his tenderness to the poor, the sick and the widowed. He used to say that he learned how to love people from a peasant. He was at an inn where two villagers sat drinking. After a while, one turned to the other: tell me, do you love me? The other said: of course I love you, with all my heart. Then tell me, what hurts me? The second shrugged. How should I know what hurts you? And the first said: if you don't know what hurts me, how can you say you love me? That's the whole story. And Moshe Leib said: from that I understood that to love someone truly is to know their need, and to carry their sorrow with them. The Torah commands, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." It's easy to hear that as a feeling. The tavern turns it into a question of attention: you can't help carry someone's hurt if you've never asked what it is. There's humility in it, too. The one who said of course I love you wasn't lying. He just hadn't looked. Moshe Leib's own life, as it's remembered, was one long answer: sitting with sick children, visiting widows, going where people hurt.
screen: `MOSHE LEIB OF SASSOV.` · `DO YOU LOVE ME? OF COURSE.` · `THEN WHAT HURTS ME?` · `LOVE AS ATTENTION.` · then, large: `KNOW WHAT HURTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you love, and honestly ask: do I know what's hurting them right now? If you do, hold it for a moment, as if carrying one corner of it; if you don't, think how you might ask them gently, without fixing anything: how are you, really? If you pray, pray for what hurts them.
Moshe Leib, the rebbe of Sassov who said he learned how to love from a peasant in a tavern: if you don't know what hurts me, how can you say you love me?
Your line: know what hurts. Love starts with the question. That's day three hundred seven.

308.title: If not higher (Peretz, 1900)
308.hook: a skeptic follows the rebbe of Nemirov at dawn and finds him chopping wood for a sick widow
308.howItsDone: Peretz's story is read in Jewish schools and often retold around the High Holy Days; it echoes the Jewish ideal of giving in secret, so that the one who receives isn't shamed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moshe Leib learned in a tavern that love means knowing what hurts.

In the town of Nemirov, the rumor was about the rebbe. Every morning in the days before the High Holy Days, when the congregation gathered before dawn to say the penitential prayers, the rebbe was missing. Where was he? His followers had an answer: he goes up to heaven, of course, to plead for us. Then a visitor from Lithuania arrived, a sharp, skeptical scholar who didn't believe a word of it. And he decided to find out.
screen: `THE REBBE IS MISSING AT DAWN.` → `HE GOES UP TO HEAVEN.` → `A SKEPTIC DECIDES TO FIND OUT.`

segments.voice: I. L. Peretz wrote this story in Yiddish, and published it in 1900. The skeptic, called the Litvak, hides under the rebbe's bed overnight. Before dawn, the rebbe gets up, and he doesn't put on his holy clothes. He puts on peasant clothes, boots and a big belt, and takes an axe and a rope. The Litvak follows him, shivering, out of town and into the woods. The rebbe chops down a small tree, splits it into logs, ties a bundle and carries it to a broken-down hut. Inside lies a poor, sick widow. The rebbe speaks like a peasant: I've got wood to sell, cheap. She says: I can't pay. He says: I'll trust you. You have a great and mighty God, and you don't trust Him for a few pennies? Then he kneels and lays the wood in her stove, and with each log he murmurs a line of the dawn prayers. He lights the fire, and leaves. The Litvak stays in Nemirov and becomes the rebbe's disciple. And from then on, when anyone says that at dawn the rebbe goes up to heaven, the Litvak doesn't laugh. He just adds, quietly: if not higher. Helping someone in secret, without credit, without even letting her know who you are, is placed above the heavens. And it closes a week of stories: the narrow bridge, the lost princess, the turkey prince, where is God, the crying baby, what hurts, and if not higher.
screen: `A LITVAK UNDER THE BED.` · `PEASANT CLOTHES AND AN AXE.` · `WOOD FOR A SICK WIDOW.` · `A PRAYER WITH EACH LOG.` · then, large: `IF NOT HIGHER.`

segments.voice: Think of one small, useful thing you could do for someone who'd never know it was you: pay for something quietly, fix what's broken, leave a kind note unsigned, refill what everyone forgets. Picture doing it and walking away without a word, notice how much of you wants credit, and let that part rest. If you pray, offer it as a prayer.
